lines.text: On the coast of North Africa, Carthage once challenged Rome, and in our own time a fruit seller's despair lit the Arab Spring. This is Tunisia.
Phoenician settlers founded Carthage on this coast, and it grew into a rich sea power, until Rome razed it to the ground.
For more than a century Rome and Carthage fought three great wars, the Punic Wars, for mastery of the western Mediterranean.
Carthage's greatest general, Hannibal, crossed the Alps with elephants and beat Rome at Cannae, before his defeat at Zama and death in exile.
Under Rome, Africa became a rich province, and at El Jem a great amphitheatre rose that still stands today.
In 670 Arab armies brought Islam, and founded the Great Mosque of Kairouan, one of the oldest in Africa.
Around it grew Kairouan, a holy city of Islam and a centre of learning for all of North Africa.
In Tunis the Zaytuna Mosque was founded, and became one of the oldest universities of the Islamic world.
From the thirteenth century the Hafsid dynasty ruled from Tunis, for more than three hundred years.
In Hafsid Tunis, Ibn Khaldun was born. His Muqaddimah studied how states rise and fall, and he is seen as an early thinker of sociology.
In 1881 France made Tunisia a protectorate, and held it for three quarters of a century.
Habib Bourguiba would lead the long struggle for independence, and become the country's first president.
Zine El Abidine Ben Ali would take power in 1987, and hold it for more than twenty years.
In 1956, after years of struggle, Tunisia won its independence from France and became a nation of its own.
That same year Bourguiba's new law banned polygamy and gave women rights rare in the Arab world.
Kais Saied, born in 1958, would become president in 2019.
In December 2010 a young street vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire in protest. His act shook the whole region.
Ons Jabeur would become the first Arab and the first African woman to reach a Grand Slam tennis final.
Within weeks of Bouazizi's protest, Tunisians drove Ben Ali from power, and the Arab Spring had begun.
When the transition faltered, four national groups brought the sides together, and won the Nobel Peace Prize for saving it.
In 2015 a gunman killed thirty-eight tourists on a beach near Sousse, a blow to the young democracy.
From Carthage to the Arab Spring, Tunisia has often been where great changes begin.
